newsitem.title: USA: Cosby story was for sale before murder-reporter.
newsitem.headline: Cosby story was for sale before murder-reporter.

text.p: A reporter for a weekly tabloid testified on Thursday a man offered to sell him a story saying Bill Cosby had an illegimate daughter and the offer came one day before the entertainer's son was murdered.

Christopher Doherty, a reporter for the Globe supermarket tabloid, testified that on Jan. 15 a man identifying himself as Jose Medina told him that he was the agent representing Autumn Jackson, who claims she is Cosby's illegimate daughter.

"Jose Medina told me that Autumn Jackson was willing to go public with her claim because her alleged father had neglected her and she wanted to come out with the story and make some money," Doherty said during the second day of testimony in the trial of Jackson, who is accused of trying to extort $40 million from Cosby.

Jackson, 22, and the other defendants, Jose Medina, 51, and Boris Sabas, 42, were accused of conspiracy, extortion and engaging in interstate commerce to commit crimes. If convicted on all counts, they could face possible prison terms of 12 years and fines of $750,000.
The entertainer's only son, Ennis, 27, was shot to death in California on Jan. 16, two days before Jackson was charged. Authorities have said the incidents are unrelated.

Doherty testified he had three conversations with Medina and at least two with Jackson in attempts to negotiate a contract. He said he was told by Medina that Jackson "was destitute and living in a car."
The reporter said he also was told that Jackson's mother Shawn Upshaw had a brief affair with Cosby and "told her daughter she had to keep it a secret."
Doherty said he became frustrated after two days of negotiations with Medina and Jackson because they kept upping the price for the story, from $5,000 to $25,000.
"Obviously, the story took on a whole new life after Ennis was murdered," Doherty said.
"We know the approximate value of this story," Medina told the reporter in a taped Jan. 16 conversation.
Later that day, Jackson telephoned the reporter and in cold, matter-of-fact tone raised the price of her story again.
"Here's the thing, okay? This is what I want. This is going to be for 50 grand when the contract comes back tomorrow," Jackson is heard saying on the tape.
She also demanded that the tabloid pay her $25,000 up front and when Doherty asked for some "leeway" in getting the money, she cooly said, "I cannot do that."

Cosby has admitted to having had an affair with Jackson's mother but has denied being her father. According to court papers, Jackson was one of many young people whose educational expenses Cosby paid for several years.
Actual paternity is not an issue in the trial.

A lawyer representing the trust set up by Cosby to pay for Jackson's living expenses and education also testified Thursday that from January 1994 to April 1995, just under $25,000 was paid on Jackson's behalf while she was enrolled in a community college in Florida. Once she dropped out of school, the trust no longer provided her with funds.
